stem: Which home-safety teaching is appropriate for parents of a young child?

options.A: Lock medicines and household cleaners out of reach, anchor unstable furniture, maintain working smoke alarms, and use appropriate outlet protection.
options.B: Store medicines on a low open shelf so the child can identify them.
options.C: Leave heavy furniture unsecured because tip-over injuries occur only in adults.
options.D: Disable smoke alarms to prevent false alarms at night.

rationale: CPSC child-safety guidance recommends securing medicines and household chemicals, anchoring furniture and televisions to reduce tip-over risk, maintaining smoke alarms, and using electrical outlet safeguards for young children.
educational_objective: Teach evidence-based household injury-prevention measures for young children.
source_document_title: Childproofing Your Home / Child Safety Guidance
source_locator: Home childproofing: medicines/cleaners locked away; furniture anchoring; smoke alarms; outlet protection
source_claim_supported: Childproofing includes secure storage of medicines/cleaners, furniture anchoring, smoke alarms, and electrical outlet protection.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance, printed p.9/PDF p.13
blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — child injury prevention
correction_summary: Consolidated current CPSC home-safety measures into a practical teaching item and removed unsupported age-specific thresholds.
